summary: The entry as a whole clears the research-interest floor. Version 1's kernel-checked answer to Kulaichev's published 1984 uniqueness question is plausibly paper-worthy: Chiodo (2021) records the question as still open, and it has an identifiable audience in certified real-algebraic computation, formal verification, and the mathematical history of the Śrī Yantra. The literature account is careful and accurate where it was checked, and it is candid that the golden slope product is the submitter's own condition with no outside source. The second theorem's research interest does not stand on its own evidence. The reason given for choosing it (that it yields the traditional 43 triangles and 24 sandhis) is not formalised. The submitter's own Table 3 lists other solid-derived fourth conditions that also give 43 triangles. The motivating constructions come only from the submitter's own unrefereed preprints.

findings.evidence: inputs/V2-kulaichev-and-golden.md: golden_unique, golden_slope; Challenge header 'Second theorem'; account section 'The golden product: where it comes from'
findings.message: The added theorem (uniqueness under Huet's conditions, Kulaichev's (b)-(d), admissibility and uv = 2√5 − 4) has no affirmatively established research audience of its own. No outside source asks for this condition. Its motivation comes from solid constructions in the submitter's unrefereed preprints (#29, #44, #103). The property that would make it interesting, that the fixed figure has the traditional 43 triangles and 24 sandhis, sits outside the Lean statement. The submitter's own account also reports (#103 Table 3) that other fourth conditions give 43 triangles as well, so the theorem does not single out the traditional figure. The entry's notability therefore rests on the Kulaichev theorem. To support the companion theorem, the account should say what a reader learns from uniqueness under this particular condition that they would not learn from the alternatives. It could also formalise the region count that motivates the condition.

internal_notes.evidence: Chiodo, C. R. Math. 359 (2021) 377-397, reference list
internal_notes.message: The bibliographic data match the account: Chiodo is the sole author, volume 359, no. 4, pp. 377-397. Chiodo cites Kulaichev 1984 (IJHS 19.3, 279-292), Huet 2002 (TCS 281, 609-628), Pustynski 2014 (IJHS 49.3, 268-277), C. S. Rao 1998 (IJHS 33.3, 203-227), Tahta 1992 (Math. Gazette 76, 49-60), Santhi et al. 2012 and Tularam 2012, all with the details the account gives. The quoted 'toujours ouverte' could not be re-read on the landing page because the full text was not fetched. It is consistent with the account.

Two construction papers that Chiodo cites are not named in the account: Bolton & Macleod, 'The geometry of the Śrīyantra', Religion 7 (1977) 66-85, and Fonseca, 'Constructive geometry of the Śrī-cakra diagram', Religion 16 (1986) 33-49. Neither is known to treat Kulaichev's uniqueness question, so this is a minor completeness point, not a finding. Naming them as checked would strengthen the account.

This second Kulaichev paper on the Sriyantra is not in the account. Its repository abstract is psychophysiological, not mathematical, so the omission is not material. It could be named among sources checked.

The search found no prior certified or formal proof of Kulaichev uniqueness besides the submitter's own work. A search summary describes Pustynski as proving 'uniqueness of the positive root of one equation'. That fits the account's description of numeric, non-certified uniqueness. The Pustynski PDF returned 404, so the p. 274 quotation and the 'two additional tiny triangles' remark could not be re-read.

internal_notes.evidence: Popular sources on Sri Yantra and the golden ratio / Great Pyramid
internal_notes.message: Popular and fringe-leaning golden-ratio claims about the Śrī Yantra exist (phi ratios, Great Pyramid slope). The submission does not invoke them and frames the golden product only as an exact algebraic condition with an explicit disclaimer. The framing is not the baseless kind named in the notability anchors. Still, a reader may associate the two, which is one more reason to tie the condition to mathematics a reader can check.

I checked the rational endpoints by exact arithmetic. Each interval has width exactly 2^-21: [0.75043828, 0.75043875] for Kulaichev and [0.67931835, 0.67931883] for the golden product. They match the stated approximations 0.7504385160 and 0.6793185887. 2√5 − 4 = 2/φ³ = (2/φ²)(1/φ) ≈ 0.4721359550, which confirms the stated product identity.

The record exists (Version 5, 20 Nov 2026). Its description states Theorems 14 and 15 and the 43/18/24 counts. Its description of Theorem 15 includes 'has the traditional form'. The Lean entry correctly leaves this out and labels the counts as certified outside Lean. The record's title and naming carry promotional wording, which is not reproduced in the blind input. That is a matter for the metadata step, not this one.
I scored Theorem 15 as if proved exactly as stated, as instructed. The planned proof is not built, and this check does not assess its feasibility.

what_would_reach_higher: State in the account why uniqueness under the golden slope product matters mathematically on its own terms, for example what it shows about the four-parameter family that the Table 3 alternatives do not, rather than resting on the traditional counts.
Formalise the region and sandhi counts (45/28 vs 43/24) in Lean, at least for the two certified figures, so the property that motivates the second theorem is part of what is checked.
Prove or certify uniqueness for one or more Table 3 alternatives, or explain why the golden product is the natural member of that class, so the choice does not look selected to reach the counts.

Add Bolton & Macleod (1977), Fonseca (1986) and Kulaichev & Ramendic (1989) to the sources-checked list, and obtain Tahta (1992) through a free route (library or interlibrary loan) to close the one unread journal source.
Seek independent reception of #103 (journal submission or citation by a specialist) so that the paper-worthiness of the companion theorem rests on more than the submitter's preprints.
Keep the golden-ratio framing strictly algebraic and avoid wording that echoes popular golden-ratio claims about the Śrī Yantra.
